html:
Ushahidi is free, open source software that collects reports from the public by text message, email and the web and plots them on a map. It was built in Kenya in early 2008, during the violence that followed the disputed election of December 2007.

During the crisis more than 1,000 people were killed and hundreds of thousands driven from their homes. The Nairobi lawyer and blogger Ory Okolloh asked online for a way to map what was happening. Within days a small group of Kenyan developers and bloggers, among them Juliana Rotich, Erik Hersman and David Kobia, built the site. The name means "testimony" or "witness" in Swahili.

The idea, later called crisis mapping, spread quickly. After the 2010 Haiti earthquake volunteers used Ushahidi to map calls for help, and it has since tracked elections, floods, wildfires and outbreaks around the world.

Ushahidi became a showcase for Kenya's tech scene, alongside M-Pesa mobile money. It showed that software used worldwide could come out of Nairobi, not only Silicon Valley.
